title: The four calls: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvar — and a fourth, mahaḥ
theme: The three ancient calls of the ritual are made the limbs of a fourth, mahaḥ, which is named Brahman and the self; each call is matched with a world, a light, a Veda and a breath.

sandhi.rule: A visarga after a vowel other than a or ā becomes r before a voiced sound: bhūḥ + bhuvaḥ → bhūr bhuvaḥ.

sandhi.type: r-final word; ai before a vowel; visarga before t; aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: suvar keeps its r before the vowel of iti. vai before e becomes vā: ai → āy by P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), and the y is dropped, leaving the hiatus vā etāḥ (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)). etāḥ before t becomes etās: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः). tisraḥ before the voiced v becomes tisro: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
saḥ loses its visarga before a vowel (as before any sound), and the hiatus stays.
i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).

morphology.note: The Taittirīya form of svar, an indeclinable whose final visarga goes back to r: pausal suvaḥ, and suvar before a vowel (suvar iti).
Causative of vid, ‘to know’: ‘causes to be known, makes known’. With sma the present reports a past event.

A patronymic: the descendant of Mahācamasa, with vṛddhi of the first syllable (mahā → māhā) and the suffix -ya. Kūranārāyaṇa names the rule of the Garga group (gargādi, yañ), cf. P. 4.1.105 (गर्गादिभ्यो यञ्).

translation.literal: Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvar — these, indeed, [are] the three calls. Of them, now, Māhācamasya made known this fourth: ‘mahaḥ’. That [is] Brahman; it [is] the self (trunk); the other deities [are its] limbs. ‘Bhūḥ’ indeed [is] this world; ‘bhuvaḥ’ the mid-region; ‘suvar’ that world [yonder].
translation.readable: Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvar: these are the three well-known calls. To them Māhācamasya added a fourth, mahaḥ. That is Brahman, the body’s trunk; the other powers are its limbs. Bhūḥ is this world, bhuvaḥ the space between, suvar the world beyond.

translation.literal: ‘Mahaḥ’ [is] the sun; by the sun, truly, all the worlds grow great. ‘Bhūḥ’ indeed [is] fire; ‘bhuvaḥ’ wind; ‘suvar’ the sun; ‘mahaḥ’ the moon; by the moon, truly, all the lights grow great. ‘Bhūḥ’ indeed [is] the Ṛg verses; ‘bhuvaḥ’ the Sāman chants; ‘suvar’ the Yajus formulas.
translation.readable: Mahaḥ is the sun, for it is the sun that makes all the worlds great. Bhūḥ is fire, bhuvaḥ wind, suvar the sun, mahaḥ the moon, for it is the moon that makes all the lights great. Bhūḥ is the verses of the Ṛgveda, bhuvaḥ the chants of the Sāmaveda, suvar the formulas of the Yajurveda.

morphology.note: catur, ‘four’, with the suffix -dhā of manner: ‘in four ways’. The four calls are each fourfold, so the anuvāka has set out sixteen equations (4 × 4).
The perfect of vid, ‘to know’, used with present meaning: ‘knows’.
Present of vah, ‘to carry’, with the preverb ā, ‘towards’: ‘they bring’.

translation.literal: ‘Mahaḥ’ [is] brahman; by brahman, truly, all the Vedas grow great. ‘Bhūḥ’ indeed [is] the out-breath; ‘bhuvaḥ’ the in-breath; ‘suvar’ the diffused breath; ‘mahaḥ’ food; by food, truly, all the breaths grow great. These four, indeed, [are] fourfold: four [and] four [are] the calls. Who knows them — he knows Brahman. To him all the gods bring tribute.
translation.readable: Mahaḥ is brahman, the syllable Om, for it is Om that makes all the Vedas great. Bhūḥ is the out-breath, bhuvaḥ the in-breath, suvar the breath that pervades the body, mahaḥ food, for it is food that makes all the breaths great. So these four calls are each fourfold: four sets of four. Whoever knows them knows Brahman; to such a person all the gods bring offerings.

syntax: Nominal sentences throughout, on the pattern ‘X iti Y’ (‘[the call] X [is] Y’), with the verb ‘to be’ understood. The opening sentence names the three calls; a narrative sentence with u ha sma and the present pravedayate (‘made known’) introduces the fourth; three short identifications (tat brahma, sa ātmā, aṅgāny anyā devatāḥ) give its rank. Then four series of four identifications follow, each closed, except the first, by a sentence explaining why the fourth member is the greatest (‘by X, truly, all Ys grow great’). The anuvāka ends with a summary (‘four, fourfold’), a relative clause of knowing (ta yo veda, sa veda brahma) and its reward.

ambiguities.note: Paired with aṅgāni, ‘limbs’, ātman may have its old bodily sense, ‘trunk’: mahaḥ is the trunk, the other calls and deities the limbs. Śaṅkara gives it the sense ‘that which pervades’ («आप्नोतेर्व्याप्तिकर्मणः आत्मा»), so that mahaḥ pervades the others; Kūranārāyaṇa the sense ‘the self that supports and governs a body’. Both readings keep the contrast of whole and parts.

In the series of Vedas (Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus), brahman stands where a fourth item of speech is expected. Śaṅkara takes it as the syllable Om («ब्रह्मेत्योङ्कारः, शब्दाधिकारे अन्यस्यासम्भवात्»), as does Kūranārāyaṇa («प्रणवेन»). It is a different use of the word from ‘tad brahma’ in the first unit and ‘sa veda brahma’ at the end.

‘Who knows them knows Brahman’ seems complete, yet Brahman was already named. Śaṅkara argues that this anuvāka and the next teach a single meditation: the next describes the Brahman to be known here («उभयोर्ह्यनुवाकयोरेकमुपासनम्»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose (brāhmaṇa style), in short clauses of the form ‘X iti Y’.

beginner: Before many Vedic rites three short words are spoken: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvar. They are old names for earth, the space above it, and the sky. This passage says that a teacher called Māhācamasya added a fourth word, mahaḥ, ‘greatness’, and that the fourth is the most important: it is the centre, and the other three are like arms and legs attached to it. Then the passage plays a matching game. In each of four groups, three things line up with the first three words, and the fourth thing is the one that makes the others great: the sun for the worlds, the moon for the stars, the sacred syllable for the Vedas, and food for the breaths of the body. Whoever understands these connections, it says, understands the highest reality.
analogy: Like a set of index cards sorted into four piles, each with a heading card on top: the passage shows that every pile — worlds, lights, scriptures, breaths — has the same four-part shape, and that in each the fourth card holds the rest together.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names three calls, bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and suvar, and reports that the sage Māhācamasya made known a fourth, mahaḥ. It says that mahaḥ is Brahman and the self, and that the other deities are limbs. It then sets out four series: worlds (this world, the mid-region, the world beyond, the sun), lights (fire, wind, sun, moon), Vedas (Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, brahman), and breaths (out-breath, in-breath, diffused breath, food). It says the four are fourfold, and that one who knows them knows Brahman and receives tribute from the gods. It does not say how the knowing is to be done; the commentators call it a meditation (upāsana).

commentary.q: Why does the text name the sage who added the fourth call?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara takes the particles u ha sma as reporting an event, and the name as part of the practice: remembering the seer is itself a limb of the meditation, since it is taught here — «माहाचमस्यग्रहणमार्षानुस्मरणार्थम्», «ऋष्यनुस्मरणमप्युपासनाङ्गमिति गम्यते, इहोपदेशात्». Nothing else is known about Māhācamasya from this edition’s sources.

commentary.q: Why is the fourth the greatest in each series?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The text gives its own reason, an etymology: mahaḥ, ‘greatness’, is the one by which the others mahīyante, ‘grow great’. Śaṅkara explains the verb as growth and increase («महनं वृद्धिः उपचयः») and the relation as that of a trunk to its limbs: «आत्मना ह्यङ्गानि महीयन्ते». He then lists the four series by call: the first call is ‘this world, fire, the Ṛgveda, the out-breath’; the fourth ‘sun, moon, brahman, food’ — «इत्येवम् एकैकाश्चतुर्धा भवन्ति».

commentary.q: Why does the anuvāka end ‘he knows Brahman’ when Brahman has been named?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara raises this objection himself and answers that the text means Brahman with the particular qualities the next anuvāka will give — that it is reached within the heart, made of mind, and so on: «तद्विशेषविवक्षुत्वाददोषः», «हृदयान्तरुपलभ्यत्वं मनोमयत्वादिश्च». So the two anuvākas form one sentence and one meditation, and the gods’ tribute is the fruit of reaching sovereignty: «स्वाराज्यप्राप्तौ सत्यामित्यर्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Vyāhṛti is an action noun from vi-ā-hṛ, ‘to utter’: an utterance, and in ritual the three short calls bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvar. Kūranārāyaṇa gives an etymology for each: bhūḥ as that in which beings come to be («भवन्त्यस्मिन् सर्वाणि भूतानीति भूः»), mahaḥ as that by which the universe is made great («महयति विश्वं, महीयते विश्वम् अनेनेति वा - महः»). Such etymologies are explanatory, not historical.

advaita.text: For Śaṅkara the Brahman meditated on through the calls is Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahman as the cosmic person, of whom the other deities are limbs: «मह इत्येतस्य हिरण्यगर्भस्य व्याहृत्यात्मनो ब्रह्मणोऽङ्गान्यन्या देवता इत्युक्तम्» (opening his comment on the next anuvāka). It is a meditation on the conditioned Brahman with a stated result, sovereignty (svārājya), not the knowledge of the unconditioned Brahman that the second vallī will teach.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa calls the meditation on the calls a limb of the meditation on the supreme that follows («परोपासनस्याङ्गभूतं व्याहृत्युपासनं»). The fourth call denotes the supreme Brahman, the whole; the others denote what is its body: «अनया चतुर्थ्या व्याहृत्या अङ्गिभूतं परं ब्रह्म प्रतिपाद्यते, अन्याभिर्व्याहृतिभिः तच्छरीरभूताः». ‘Self’ means the one who supports and rules all things as a soul does its body: «यथैकस्य शरीरस्य शरीरि तथा सर्वेषां भूतानाम् आत्मा». In the solar series he takes mahaḥ as Nārāyaṇa within the sun («आदित्यान्तवर्ती नारायणः»).

dvaita.text: Madhva’s comment consists of verses he attributes to a work he calls Vyāhṛtitattva («इति व्याहृतितत्त्वे»). In them the four calls name four forms of Viṣṇu: Aniruddha (bhūḥ, the head), Pradyumna (bhuvaḥ, the arms), Saṅkarṣaṇa (suvar, the feet) and Vāsudeva (mahaḥ, the middle of the body) — «वासुदेवो महोनामा त्वनिरुद्धश्शिरो मतः». Māhācamasya is the god Brahmā, who knows them: «माहाचमस्यस्तज्ज्ञानी ब्रह्मा सम्परिकीर्तितः». These are verses cited by Madhva; this edition cannot verify them as quotations of an independent work.

schools.disagreement: All read the four calls as a meditation in which mahaḥ is the whole and the rest its parts. They differ on what that whole is: Hiraṇyagarbha, the conditioned Brahman, for Śaṅkara; the supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, with the rest as its body, for Kūranārāyaṇa; and for Madhva Viṣṇu in four forms, with Māhācamasya as Brahmā.

parallels.quote: तस्य भूरिति शिर एकं शिर एकमेतदक्षरं
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka also lays the calls on a body — bhūḥ the head, bhuvaḥ the arms, svar the feet — of the person in the sun. Madhva cites this passage in his comment.
The next anuvāka uses the same correspondences (bhūḥ — fire, bhuvaḥ — wind, suvar — sun, mahaḥ — brahman) for the path of the one who meditates.

contemporary.text: The passage describes a whole whose centre does not replace its parts but makes them ‘grow great’: the sun does not abolish the worlds, food does not compete with the breaths. Leaders often think of the centre of an organisation as the place where decisions are taken away from the parts. The image here is different: the centre is judged by whether the parts flourish because of it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Think of something in your life that holds other things together — a habit, a person, a place. What grows because of it?
reflect.deeper: Why might a teaching about Brahman begin with lists of correspondences rather than with a definition?
reflect.practice: Write four things you do each day and ask which of them makes the other three possible. Notice whether you give that one the most attention.

references.text: Kūranārāyaṇa’s commentary in the six-commentary edition prints a footnote quoting Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s bhāṣya on vyāhṛti; Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara is not among this edition’s sources and is not cited here.

flags.note: Madhva’s text writes svar for the Taittirīya suvar (corrections.json, orthographic); the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha writes a visarga before a sibilant as that sibilant. Neither changes the meaning.
The identification of the Brahman meditated on here (Hiraṇyagarbha, the supreme, or Viṣṇu in four forms) is a matter of school; the text names it only as ‘mahaḥ … Brahman … the self’.
